newsitem.title: India: India steps up evacuation as cyclone kills two.
newsitem.headline: India steps up evacuation as cyclone kills two.

text.p: Authorities on Wednesday evacuated more than 300,000 people to safety in the southeastern state of Andhra Pradesh as a powerful cyclone, moving towards its coast, claimed its first two victims.
Officials in the state capital Hyderabad said one person was killed in a house collapse and the other was crushed under an uprooted tree as strong winds swept the coast ahead of the storm.
Meteorological officials said the storm, with gale force winds of up to 180 kmph (113 miles per hour), was moving in a northwesterly direction in the Bay of Bengal towards the coast.
They said the cyclone was expected to cross land between Ongole town and Kakinada port at about 2.00 a.m. on Thursday (2030 GMT Wednesday).
Officials said the cyclone, which was earlier expected to hit Andhra Pradesh around noon, had slowed down in its advance.
"It is quite worrying that it is slowing down...it seems to be intensifying further," said J.V.M Naidu, director of the cyclone warning centre at Visakhapatnam port.
Officials said more than 300,000 people from 600 villages on the coast had been moved to 700 relief camps in the five districts of East and West Godavari, Krishna, Prakasam and Guntur.
"I can say with confidence that all women and children have been brought out of the coastal areas," said Chitra Ramachandran, administrator of the Krishna district.

Ramachandran said a 90 km (55.92 miles)-long and 15-km (9.321 miles) wide strip of the coast had been declared a "no-man's zone" as the storm, second in a month, threatened to rip through villages lying in its path.

Coastal areas in Andhra Pradesh were devastated by a storm in early November that left more than 2,000 people dead or missing at sea. It damaged crops and property worth more than 50 billion rupees ($1.4 billion).
Most of the damage was in the two districts of East and West Godavari. The two deaths from the latest storm were reported from East Godavari.
Officials fear the latest cyclone could cause more damage to property and crops than the previous one.
"The second sowing season has just begun. A storm is the worst thing that can happen now," said an official.

Officials said they expected the storm to whip up winds of 150-180 kmh (94-113 miles per hour) and tidal waves two to three metres high (six to nine feet) which are expected to flood low-lying areas up to 10 km (six miles) inland.

Port officials in Kakinada said they had moved nine ships out of the harbour to avoid their being buffeted by the rough seas. Rail and road services were suspended and power switched off in areas likely to be affected by the cyclone.
